transcript: If I said to you, "Save our bacon." the Save our bacon act, you might think, well, someone is going to be helped by that. It's helping consumers or it's helping farmers or someone. But, the Save our bacon act is really about helping some of the biggest agricultural corporations in the country. It's quite a scam. I recently spoke with Jake Davis, the president of Uproot, which is bringing this fight to the forefront. We talked about the Save our bacon act. We talked about why critics say it's a big win for big ag, and how it could affect food standards in your state. Let's check out this conversation. Jake Davis is the president of Uproot. You know, Jake, we've been following very closely all aspects of both the regulatory environment and food safety at the state and federal level. And one thing I find interesting is we're hearing a lot out of Washington about we've got to make food healthier and safer, but we see staffing cuts, we see reorgs, concerns about food safety experts saying there's reduced oversight capability here. And against this kind of backdrop, Congress is now considering this legislation, which would arguably make it harder for a state to say, "Hey, we want to have higher standards in some areas, including food production." Do you see what is happening with this particular bill as being related to these broader changes I've pointed out coming out of DC? Are these things related? >> Yeah, definitely we're seeing a a connection between the sort of corporate overreach and the influ- influence of what we sort of call big ag, the industry as a whole. Those corporations that dominate much of the market are, you know, quietly behind the scenes rewriting a wide range of rules that that benefit them, right? That are specifically designed to make it easier for them to operate without additional standards, to make it easier for them to prevent future um you know, for prevent states in the future from making it harder for them to do exactly what they want to do to maximize profits and minimize safety. >> When you hear the name Save Our Bacon Act, it sounds kind of good, right? I mean, like someone must be getting helped by this. Maybe it's consumers or maybe it's farmers or something like that, but it's really quite a misleading name, isn't it? >> Yeah, it's a very misleading name. The The truth is is that it doesn't save anybody's bacon or maybe the only folks that saves bacon is the big corporations who want to minimize any future standards, the current ones, but anything in addition to what they currently have to deal with. And And the truth is it will drive out independent family farmers like me who, you know, raise uh pork and pigs at in a with higher standards and get access to these kinds of markets. It'll make it harder for consumers to find the kinds of high-quality foods that they want because the truth is this is a race to the bottom. Uh so, the the idea that it's saving the American people's bacon, it's saving farmers bacon, the truth is it's really just helping corporations rake in profits. >> There's a states' rights kind of conundrum in the background of this where California had Proposition 12. And which would have raised and established minimum standards in California uh for animal treatment. Big Ag didn't like it. They took it all the way to the Supreme Court. They lost there. And then now they're trying this legislative approach. And it's sort of weird to me because they lost this fight with voters. They lost this fight with judges and now they're going to Congress at a time when I mean listen, maybe it is a maybe it's strategically it's an opportune time for them to go to Congress and they're going to try to win this a different way kind of ignoring the rights of states to decide what's best for them. >> Yeah, that's exactly right. You know, they claim that the the you know, the folks at the top of these corporations, folks in the sort of big ag infrastructure claim that they want to do what consumers want and that they want to provide the products that consumers want but it was pretty darn clear when California voters voted that they wanted higher standards for how animals were raised. They wanted animals out of these cruel inhumane disgusting overcrowded environments. They wanted them out of gestation crates. They didn't want mother pigs spending their entire lives virtually in these spaces. But when voters said that their first reaction was we we we've lost at the ballot box. Now let's go to the court. Then when they lost at the court and by the way I'll I'll I'll say a conservative court ruled against this, right? A conservative Supreme Court ruled against this yet they continued to come back time after time, spend money on lobbyists, put as much pressure on you know, elected officials as possible to overturn the will of the people. I mean, that is why Uproot is in this fight is that we believe that decisions around our food should be driven by people, not corporations and those corporations just keep fighting. Anytime they get turned back, they just keep fighting and keep fighting and this is a last gasp effort of them to to try to continue to change those rules in their favor. If I try to steel man or make the strongest possible case for those who say this it it would be a good thing to ban state minimum standards. What I'm seeing is sort of a price argument, which is listen, a lot of people are struggling with the cost of food. There were promises made that groceries were going to get really cheap under this administration, but inflation has continued. Why would we allow states to do something which would simply raise the price that consumers at the end of the day pay? Why That seems to be the strongest argument, although I don't know that that's a good argument for reducing food standards to me. But but is that the the main argument that the proponents are making? >> That's certainly the argument they're making, although oddly in in ways, if you look at who is fighting back against this legislation, it's small independent family farmers. It's you know, it's consumers. It's it's folks that would be hurt by this. And the on the office on the opposition side, you've got just a few big corporations that control, you know, Smithfield for example, a Chinese-owned corporation. They own they they control one in four pigs in the US, right? About 25% of the market. And they're one of the biggest proponents of saying we don't we we want to overturn California's rules. That doesn't say to me those corporations that are setting the price today that they're in some way miraculously going to bring down prices whenever we we say no more food safety standards, for example. The truth is is that consoli- we know like the the economics are true. We know that when you consolidate a market, what happens is maybe prices dip for a second, but ultimately those corporations that then control all of the market and have no competition, they then immediately continue to raise those prices. And I would even argue to some degree gouge consumers when when you know, they have a full control of the market, and they've pushed everyone else out. >> If people haven't heard of Proposition 12 or haven't heard of the Save Our Bacon Act or just learning about this now, if this passes, what changes for just the average American who grocery shops? >> Yeah. So, Proposition 12 set some very minimum standards for for folks in California that pork and and other animal products, eggs, veal calves, those sorts of things can't be sold in the state if they don't meet some very minimal standards around food safety and space requirements. What What would ultimately change for everyone else is that they would lose hundreds of state laws that govern basic food production standards in all kinds of other places as well, and they would lose the right to when who knows what happens in the future, right? We're dealing with all kinds of things in agriculture right now. We're dealing with bird flu, we're dealing with screwworms, like they're dealing with all different kinds of things. >> Yeah. >> We don't know what kind of state standards we might need in the future, but if we give away this opportunity today, if if the Save Our Bacon Act passes, then what happens is states actually can't come back and pass any laws in the future that might address those new developing issues in a very changing world. It seems like a a crazy trade-off to me to take away those states' rights to address things that are happening in their states for a few corporations. >> Yeah, if you zoom out a little bit, there's the fight about pork. There's the fight about forward-looking standards related to pork, for example, but there is a bigger fight here, I would say, about whether giant corporations get to overrule voters when they don't like the outcome. That seems to be what's at stake, bigger picture here. Correct me if I'm wrong. >> No, you're exactly right. And look, this is a precedent that if, you know, these giant companies in the food sector win that fight, other people are looking at this fight. Other corporations in other sectors of our economy are looking at that fight and they're saying, "Okay, if we can control the federal government, if we can control Congress, if we can influence what they can do, it's a lot better for us to move the power of the people from the local voters up to those people that, frankly, our lobbyists can have a lot more influence over. And so, those corporations in all kinds of sectors of our economy are watching this fight, and ultimately, they're seeing how this is going to play out in in whether we're ready as a country to let corporations have free reign of setting our food standards, even when voters overwhelmingly said these were the food standards they wanted. >> We're going to tell people in a moment what can be done and sort of the trajectory of this bill, but for those who are saying, "Well, I don't know that this affects me. I I'm not sure that I'm directly implicated." Think of a future where voters want stronger standards. It could be for food safety, it could be for animal treatment, it could be for labeling. There's a whole bunch of other areas. Why on earth would we be okay with a law that says voters can't decide that that's what what's best for them? That seems extraordinarily dangerous to me, which gets us to give us the timeline of the next few weeks in Congress, and if if people are hearing this and they're saying, "Hey, that sounds bad. I want to get involved. What can people do?" >> Yeah, we know that the House uh of Representatives has already passed their farm bill. It includes the Save Our Bacon language in the farm bill. It's a a small provision that was pushed in there um really at the uh behest of corporations. And we now know the Senate is taking up their version of the farm bill. Language of that Senate version is coming out soon. If it if not by the time we're uh on the air with this, it may already be out. And then there's going to be a Senate Agriculture Committee markup of this issue. And that is one of the most important places that the Save Our Bacon Act could be pushed into the farm bill. And if corporate lobbyists have their way, they will try to push that through an amendment process through ensuring it's in in text of the bill. What can people do about that? The first thing they can do is they can sign a petition that we have uh at Uproot to tell Big Pork to stop pushing this against the will of the people. We need to tell those corporations that frankly we buy from every day to step back and to stop pushing on this issue. Uh I'll tell you I'm calling my senator and I'm asking them to to not vote for this bill. So um I think that those are the things that that we should really be thinking about as as folks watching your show. >> So this has now become a Senate fight. It is the Senate that we need to focus on if we want to make a difference here. >> That's right. >> We have been speaking Yeah, go ahead, Jake. >> Well, I was just going to say and and the the the the main thing that we have to do is to make our voices heard in this space because big agriculture corporations, these meat corporations, they know the American people are not, you know, they're out at their 4th of July cookouts. They're not paying as much attention to this issue and they're ready to to cram this through and make sure that they get what they want out of this. So, right now is an opportunity to make our voices heard. >> That's right. They're hoping that no one will pay attention, no one will think there's implications serious enough to get involved and that's that's exactly what we're trying trying to dissuade people of that notion. Jake Davis, president of Uproot, thanks for your time. We're covering it. We're going to keep talking about it. >> Thanks for having me, David.
